items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Ralph Gleason, when he was writing for the San Francisco Chronicle, wrote a wonderful column on what you just remarked on. He said some day in the future, sociologists will refer to Jon Hendricks’ lyrics... And I thought — I was very flattered by that.

ctx.x: And it’s like a vocabulary lesson in what was happening at the time. I mean what do they call this, this kind of language? Or maybe it didn’t have a name? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

Then it didn’t have a name. Leonard Feather gave it the name “vocalese.” And that stuck. But Ralph Gleason, when he was writing for the San Francisco Chronicle, wrote a wonderful column on what you just remarked on. He said some day in the future, sociologists will refer to Jon Hendricks’ lyrics to see how people spoke in the 50s and 60s. And I thought — I was very flattered by that. It was very flattering. But I think it’s true. Because the lyrics are full of vulgate expressions that were very much in use at one…
And you had quite a wonderful association with Count Basie.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Even when he criticized Lambert, Hendricks, and Ross for the Duke Ellington album, I accepted it. I said, “You’re right, Ralph. That’s exactly right.” And I told him when I saw him.

ctx.x: That’s true. Did criticism ever really affect you?

No, because I knew whether it was accurate or not. Ralph Gleason, whatever he said, always affected me, because I know that it was true what he said. Even when he criticized Lambert, Hendricks, and Ross for the Duke Ellington album, I accepted it. I said, “You’re right, Ralph. That’s exactly right.” And I told him when I saw him. I said, “Dead on,” because he could hear, and he spoke the truth. But most of them, today especially, I find that they are abysmal, abysmal. They lack any literary ethics. They don’t…

I got this tape. It says, “Hello. This is Peter Watrous. Leave a name and your number, and maybe I’ll call you back.” I said, who is this little pompous jackass? I couldn’t believe it. So I said on the tape, I said, “Peter, this is Jon Hendricks, and first I want to tell you a little bit about myself.
